steps.why: Hardness is about shape, not only about strength. A covalent bond points in a fixed direction, so every atom in diamond is locked into position by four such directions at once and the shape of the crystal cannot be changed without breaking bonds.
common_mistakes: Answering sp² for diamond. Each carbon is bonded to four other carbon atoms, so it is sp³.
Describing diamond as layers of atoms. Layers belong to graphite; diamond is a three-dimensional network.
steps.memory_tip: Four bonds in fixed directions build a rigid network.
steps.margin_note: Describe the tetrahedral arrangement before giving the reason.

lines.text: A rigid covalent network makes it hard

steps.why: The contrast with graphite is what makes this convincing. Graphite is the same element with the same kind of covalent bonds, and it is soft only because it has weak forces between sliding sheets. Diamond has no such weak direction anywhere.
common_mistakes: Saying diamond is hard only because carbon is a small atom. Small size helps make the bonds short and strong, but the hardness comes from the rigid network of four bonds per atom.
Giving the same reason here as for graphite's softness. Graphite is soft because its sheets slide; diamond has no sheets to slide.
steps.memory_tip: Nothing is weak and nothing slides, so nothing moves out of place.
steps.margin_note: Contrast with graphite in one line; it shows why the three-dimensional network matters.

insider_note: A complete answer describes the rigid three-dimensional network of four covalent bonds per carbon and then says there are no weak forces and no sliding layers anywhere in diamond.
